units.translation: The example from Aeschylus is uncertain because of the corruption of the adjoining words. It is certain that ἐπάμιδα [a word of uncertain meaning] is corrupted from ἐπ᾽ ἄμαλα [upon the sheaves], which Hermann restored. For αἵμονες ὡς [bloody ones, as] Turnebus wrote αἵμονίζω σ' [I make you bloody], from the scholiast's note ἡμαγμένον [having been bloodied] (correctly ήμαγμένην [having been bloodied, feminine] according to Weil) σε καθίζω [I seat you].
bloody ones, as upon the sheaves,
to say, to advise, to command, to praise, to approve, to be content, to acquiesce, i.e. allow to go out
to approve, to be content, to acquiesce
Of these things you may say what is both possible and right to praise.
Or you praise a great and heavy-wrathful divinity in this house.
How shall I praise these things openly?
I approve of hiding these agreements of mine.
I approve of doing these things as one accountable.
From where they approved calling the people Kouretes.
But you wish to praise or blame me.
May you praise neither a life without rule nor one ruled by a master.
I praise the male in all things.
I praise the words of these prayers.
Having learned, I know how to praise the race.
For having done these things in you everywhere, I will praise.
Unless someone goes to the ship having approved these things.
I praise the better of evil and the two-thirds share, and that justice follows justice.
You praised the great-boasting divinity going from the house,
from riddles with dark oracles, helpless.
I will instruct no longer from riddles.
I understood the word from riddles.
clearly and not at all in riddling manner.
not at all in riddling manner.
having an unfortunate marriage-bed, unfortunate in marriage
having an unfortunate marriage-bed, unfortunate in marriage

Lycophron 1354 said κευθμώνος αἰνόλεκτρον μυχόν [the dread-marriage-bed recess of the hiding-place], αἰνολεχής [dread-marriage-bed] in the Orphic poems, αἰνόγαμος [dread-marriage] in the same place and in Euripides.
the dread-marriage-bed recess of the hiding-place
through which strife came to those who died horribly.

Orestes about Agamemnon, where the sense requires αἰνοπαθές [having suffered dreadfully], which Hartung restored and perhaps the scholiast read, who interprets it as δεινά παθών [having suffered terrible things].
an evil tale of ruinous fortune;
not honoring the power of wealth, marked falsely by praise.
Let praise hold this city of the Pelasgians.

The adjective αἶνά [dreadful], used adverbially, for δεινά [terrible], I conjectured should be restored at line 576 for reasons set out in Philologus vol. 13 p. 489. I added αἰνῶν [of dread things] at Ag. 153 after νεικέων [of quarrels].
dreadfully, dreadfully, it is bent upon the knee.
black smoke, the swift-moving sister of fire.
of varied mouth, of changeful speech
